cumulative_memories.memory_text: The doctor told me he might switch me to Zoloft or Lexapro and have me take it twice a day instead of once.
grounded_facts: The doctor considers switching Hazel's medication to Zoloft or Lexapro with increased frequency.

cumulative_memories.memory_text: When the doctor suggested increasing my medication, I shot back with 'Why stop there?' and said I could take it—I'm like the Keith Richards of cancer kids.
grounded_facts: Hazel sarcastically responds to the doctor's suggestion of increasing medication, comparing herself to Keith Richards.

cumulative_memories.memory_text: I was there with my mom and the doctor, talking about my mental health and treatment options, and later he asked if I’d been going to that support group.
grounded_facts: A medical consultation involving Hazel, her mother Frannie, and the doctor, focusing on mental health and treatment options.

cumulative_memories.memory_text: I challenged the doctor when he called my illness a 'journey'—I said, 'Journey? Really?'—because that word felt fake and overused, like it was supposed to make everything sound meaningful.
grounded_facts: Hazel challenges the doctor's use of the word 'journey' to describe illness, showing resistance to euphemistic language.

cumulative_memories.memory_text: I remember the doctor asking me again about going to that support group he suggested, and I told him I wasn't sure it was for me, but he kept pushing, saying it would help me connect with others.
grounded_facts: The doctor raises the topic of Hazel attending the suggested support group, prompting resistance and skepticism.

cumulative_memories.memory_text: I remember the doctor dismissing what I said and insisting I try the support group, ending with 'For me'—so I felt I had to agree, even though I didn't want to.
grounded_facts: The doctor dismisses Hazel's protest and insists she try the support group, appealing to personal obligation.

cumulative_memories.memory_text: I sat in the church basement during the support group, listening to Patrick talk about being in the heart of Jesus 'literally' while I thought about how he's just exploiting his cancer past, surviving ball cancer but now divorced and addicted to video games, and expecting us to believe we could be like him one day.
grounded_facts: Hazel participates in a cancer support group meeting in a church basement, where members share their cancer stories.

cumulative_memories.memory_text: I shared a knowing look with Isaac, my only friend here, when Patrick was speaking—we both rolled our eyes at how insincere it felt.
grounded_facts: Hazel and Isaac exchange a knowing look of disapproval toward Patrick's speech.

cumulative_memories.memory_text: I remember Patrick gesturing for me to speak, and I felt that familiar dread as I reluctantly stood up.
grounded_facts: Patrick calls on Hazel to share her story during the support group session.

cumulative_memories.memory_text: I told the group, 'I'm, uh, Hazel. 16. Thyroid originally but with quite the impressive satellite colony in my lungs,' and my voice sounded distant to me.
grounded_facts: Hazel verbally discloses her thyroid cancer with lung metastases during the support group session.

cumulative_memories.memory_text: After I shared, I heard everyone say together, 'We're here for you,' and I remember thinking how strange it was that they said it like they meant it.
grounded_facts: The group collectively says 'We're here for you' after Hazel shares her story.

cumulative_memories.memory_text: I was in the church basement with the others, going through the motions of the support group while Patrick led us in saying 'We're here for you'—first for him, then for me.
grounded_facts: A gathering of young cancer patients in a church basement led by Patrick, where members share personal experiences with cancer.

cumulative_memories.memory_text: I came out of the church and got in the car, and when Frannie looked at me like she wanted to know how it went, I just exhaled—I didn’t have the energy to say anything.
grounded_facts: Hazel comes out of the church and gets into the car without speaking, only exhaling in response to Frannie's silent question.
Frannie looks at Hazel with a questioning expression; Hazel responds only with an exhale, conveying ambivalence or fatigue.

cumulative_memories.memory_text: I just exhaled and got in the car after the group session inside the church.
grounded_facts: A group session takes place inside the church, which Frannie waits for to end and Hazel participates in.

cumulative_memories.memory_text: I remember my mom suggesting I call my friends, but I told her that's okay, I didn't feel like it.
grounded_facts: Frannie suggests Hazel call her friends, but Hazel dismisses the idea indifferently.

cumulative_memories.memory_text: I suggested to my parents that they go to a movie, telling them they haven't been out in a while and they should take the night off to have fun.
grounded_facts: Hazel proposes that her parents go to a movie, encouraging them to take a break from staying home and attending to her.

cumulative_memories.memory_text: When my dad asked if I wanted to see a movie, I told them they should go instead and have some time to themselves.
grounded_facts: Michael asks if Hazel wants to see a movie, but she redirects the idea to her parents instead.

cumulative_memories.memory_text: I remember sitting on the couch with my book while 'America's Next Top Model' played, and my parents watched me quietly, not saying much.
grounded_facts: A Friday night family gathering in the living room, centered around passive TV watching and unspoken concern for Hazel.

cumulative_memories.memory_text: I remember thinking that support group was the worst idea, and I told my parents they couldn't make me go, though I guess they can since they're my parents.
grounded_facts: A scheduled gathering for individuals with shared experiences to provide mutual support, which Hazel is being sent to attend.

cumulative_memories.memory_text: My parents insisted I needed to get out of the house and be a teenager, so they made me go to support group despite my objections.
grounded_facts: Hazel's parents insist she attend a support group, overriding her objections.

cumulative_memories.memory_text: I told my parents that if they really wanted me to be a teenager, they should buy me a fake ID so I could go to clubs and drink gimlets instead of going to support group.
grounded_facts: Hazel sarcastically rejects the idea of attending support group and suggests getting a fake ID instead.

cumulative_memories.memory_text: Frannie ended the argument by telling me to get in the car, so I knew the discussion was over.
grounded_facts: Frannie ends the discussion by ordering Hazel to get in the car.

cumulative_memories.memory_text: I saw the small Episcopalian sanctuary in suburban Indianapolis when I got out of the car with my mom's help, oxygen tank in tow.
grounded_facts: A church service taking place at an Episcopalian sanctuary in suburban Indianapolis.

cumulative_memories.memory_text: I went to the church service not because I wanted to or thought it would help, but to make my parents happy, like most things I did these days.
grounded_facts: Hazel goes to a church service at an Episcopalian sanctuary, not out of personal desire but to please her parents.

cumulative_memories.memory_text: I heard my mom shout 'Make some friends!' as she got back in the car, but I didn't feel like engaging with anyone.
grounded_facts: Frannie shouts a suggestion to Hazel to make friends before leaving.

cumulative_memories.memory_text: I decided to take the stairs instead of the elevator after seeing that very sick child.
grounded_facts: Hazel chooses to take the stairs instead of the elevator after encountering a very sick child.

cumulative_memories.memory_text: I said 'Sorry!' when we bumped into each other, and he replied with 'My bad. No, it's...'—we both apologized so quickly, like we were trying to fix it before it even started.
grounded_facts: After bumping into each other, Gus and Hazel exchange brief, polite apologies.

cumulative_memories.memory_text: I walked right into a supremely beautiful boy, and for a moment, I couldn't speak—I just felt this intense awareness between us before I managed to shuffle away.
grounded_facts: Hazel collides with Gus, a strikingly attractive boy, leading to a moment of mutual awareness and speechlessness.

cumulative_memories.memory_text: I looked in the mirror and didn't like what I saw, feeling a wave of discomfort and self-disapproval.
grounded_facts: Hazel looks in the mirror and reacts negatively to her own appearance, indicating self-disapproval or distress.

cumulative_memories.memory_text: I sat in the Circle of Sick, surrounded by others who, like me, were just trying to get through another day.
grounded_facts: A gathering of cancer patients in a church basement for sharing experiences and emotional support.

cumulative_memories.memory_text: I heard Isaac say he was facing another surgery soon and that it would likely leave him blind, and I remember how he tried to downplay it, but I could feel how much it weighed on him.
grounded_facts: Isaac reveals he will undergo another surgery soon and will likely become blind as a result.

cumulative_memories.memory_text: I felt the Beautiful Boy's gaze on me while Isaac was talking, and it was hard to focus, so I decided to meet his stare head-on.
grounded_facts: Hazel meets Augustus's persistent stare with equal intensity, initiating a silent contest of wills.

cumulative_memories.memory_text: I think I won the staring contest with him because I held my gaze just as firmly, even though I can't be totally sure he gave up first.
grounded_facts: Hazel initiates and wins a silent staring contest with Augustus after feeling his persistent gaze.

cumulative_memories.memory_text: I remember Augustus introducing himself, saying he was 17 and had lost a leg to osteosarcoma a year and a half ago, but was now in remission.
grounded_facts: Augustus reveals his name, age, and cancer history, including losing a leg to osteosarcoma and being in remission.

cumulative_memories.memory_text: I heard Augustus say he wants to live an extraordinary life and be remembered, and that his greatest fear is not doing that — it's oblivion.
grounded_facts: Augustus states that his greatest fear is oblivion, because he wants to live an extraordinary life and be remembered.

cumulative_memories.memory_text: I told Augustus that oblivion is inevitable for everyone, even people like Cleopatra or Mozart, and that fearing it doesn't make sense because eventually no one will remember any of us anyway.
grounded_facts: Hazel argues that oblivion is inevitable for everyone, and that fearing it is pointless because even great historical figures will eventually be forgotten.
Hazel publicly responds to Augustus's fear of oblivion by arguing it is inevitable and should be ignored.

cumulative_memories.memory_text: I heard the doctor say I'm depressed, even though I kept saying I'm not, and it felt like no one was listening to me.
grounded_facts: The doctor asserts that Hazel is depressed despite her repeated denials.

cumulative_memories.memory_text: I was there in the living room with my mom and the doctor, sitting through another appointment where they talked about my condition while I just wanted to go back to my book.
grounded_facts: A medical appointment where Hazel's condition is discussed by her mother and the doctor.

cumulative_memories.memory_text: I narrated that my depression isn't a side effect of cancer—it's a side effect of dying.
grounded_facts: Hazel narrates that her depression is not due to cancer but to the fact of dying.

cumulative_memories.memory_text: I kept telling myself and everyone else that I'm not depressed, because I know my feelings come from the reality of dying, not from the cancer itself.
grounded_facts: Hazel repeatedly insists she is not depressed, countering the doctor's diagnosis.

cumulative_memories.memory_text: I looked up from my book when I heard a laugh, saw a guy spinning a girl around playfully, and then I went back to reading.

cumulative_memories.memory_text: The doctor told me he might switch me to Zoloft or Lexapro and have me take it twice a day instead of once.
grounded_facts: The doctor considers switching Hazel's medication to Zoloft or Lexapro with increased frequency.

cumulative_memories.memory_text: When the doctor suggested increasing my medication, I shot back with 'Why stop there?' and said I could take it—I'm like the Keith Richards of cancer kids.

cumulative_memories.memory_text: I was there with my mom and the doctor, talking about my mental health and treatment options, and later he asked if I’d been going to that support group.
grounded_facts: A medical consultation involving Hazel, her mother Frannie, and the doctor, focusing on mental health and treatment options.

cumulative_memories.memory_text: I challenged the doctor when he called my illness a 'journey'—I said, 'Journey? Really?'—because that word felt fake and overused, like it was supposed to make everything sound meaningful.
grounded_facts: Hazel challenges the doctor's use of the word 'journey' to describe illness, showing resistance to euphemistic language.

cumulative_memories.memory_text: I remember the doctor asking me again about going to that support group he suggested, and I told him I wasn't sure it was for me, but he kept pushing, saying it would help me connect with others.
grounded_facts: The doctor raises the topic of Hazel attending the suggested support group, prompting resistance and skepticism.

cumulative_memories.memory_text: I remember the doctor dismissing what I said and insisting I try the support group, ending with 'For me'—so I felt I had to agree, even though I didn't want to.
grounded_facts: The doctor dismisses Hazel's protest and insists she try the support group, appealing to personal obligation.

cumulative_memories.memory_text: I sat in the church basement during the support group, listening to Patrick talk about being in the heart of Jesus 'literally' while I thought about how he's just exploiting his cancer past, surviving ball cancer but now divorced and addicted to video games, and expecting us to believe we could be like him one day.
grounded_facts: Hazel participates in a cancer support group meeting in a church basement, where members share their cancer stories.

cumulative_memories.memory_text: I shared a knowing look with Isaac, my only friend here, when Patrick was speaking—we both rolled our eyes at how insincere it felt.
grounded_facts: Hazel and Isaac exchange a knowing look of disapproval toward Patrick's speech.

cumulative_memories.memory_text: I remember Patrick gesturing for me to speak, and I felt that familiar dread as I reluctantly stood up.
grounded_facts: Patrick calls on Hazel to share her story during the support group session.

cumulative_memories.memory_text: I told the group, 'I'm, uh, Hazel. 16. Thyroid originally but with quite the impressive satellite colony in my lungs,' and my voice sounded distant to me.

cumulative_memories.memory_text: After I shared, I heard everyone say together, 'We're here for you,' and I remember thinking how strange it was that they said it like they meant it.

cumulative_memories.memory_text: I was in the church basement with the others, going through the motions of the support group while Patrick led us in saying 'We're here for you'—first for him, then for me.

cumulative_memories.memory_text: I could barely breathe, and I saw my dad call 9-1-1 while Frannie stroked my hair.

cumulative_memories.memory_text: I felt Frannie running her fingers through my hair as I struggled to breathe, trying to calm me down before the procedure.

cumulative_memories.memory_text: I remember my mom Frannie asking me tearfully if I was ready, her voice trembling as she leaned close, and I could tell she was trying to stay strong for me.

cumulative_memories.memory_text: I remember Gus teasing me, saying I must be a college girl and that’s why I have this ‘aura of sophistication,’ after I told him I had my GED.
grounded_facts: Gus playfully attributes Hazel's sophistication to her being a college girl after learning she has her GED.

cumulative_memories.memory_text: I smiled back at Gus and gave him a light shove on his arm, just playful enough to feel like we were really starting to ease into each other.

cumulative_memories.memory_text: I saw Gus roll his eyes when he called his parents' plaques 'encouragements,' and I could tell he meant it affectionately but also a little mockingly.
grounded_facts: Gus rolls his eyes when explaining his parents' engraved plaques as 'encouragements', signaling mild embarrassment or affectionate mockery to Hazel.

cumulative_memories.memory_text: When I arrived at Gus's house, I noticed his parents were already busy making dinner in the kitchen.
grounded_facts: Gus's parents are preparing dinner in the kitchen when Hazel arrives with Gus.

cumulative_memories.memory_text: Gus introduced me to his parents in the kitchen, and I realized they didn’t seem surprised to see him with a girl, which I made a mental note of.
grounded_facts: Gus brings Hazel into his house and introduces her to his parents, who are making dinner in the kitchen.

cumulative_memories.memory_text: When Gus introduced me as 'Hazel Grace,' I corrected him and said it's just 'Hazel,' because that's what I go by.
grounded_facts: Hazel clarifies that she goes by 'Hazel', not 'Hazel Grace', asserting her preferred identity.

cumulative_memories.memory_text: After the quick introduction, Gus abruptly said we were going downstairs and then pulled me into the next room, leaving his parents behind.
grounded_facts: Gus abruptly ends the parental introduction and pulls Hazel downstairs, redirecting focus to private time together.

cumulative_memories.memory_text: I followed Gus downstairs to his basement bedroom, and I saw it was filled with video games, band posters, and basketball memorabilia—he even pointed out what was really his and what he called 'cancer perks.'
grounded_facts: Gus leads Hazel downstairs to his basement bedroom, revealing personal space filled with video games, band posters, and basketball memorabilia.

cumulative_memories.memory_text: I struggled to breathe after walking down the stairs and had to sit on Gus's bed to recover—I told him I'd be fine unless I fainted, joking that I'm a bit of a Victorian lady that way.
grounded_facts: Hazel struggles with breathing after descending stairs and standing, requiring rest on Gus's bed.

cumulative_memories.memory_text: I told Gus that 'An Imperial Affliction' is my favorite novel—my bible, really—and that its author understands what it’s like to be dying without having died, which means something deep to me.
grounded_facts: Hazel names 'An Imperial Affliction' as her favorite novel, describing it as deeply meaningful and spiritually significant to her.

cumulative_memories.memory_text: I saw that Gus decided to read 'An Imperial Affliction' even though he wasn’t sure about it at first, and I realized he was trying to understand my world.
grounded_facts: Gus commits to reading 'An Imperial Affliction' despite initial skepticism, marking a shift in his attitude toward Hazel's inner world.

cumulative_memories.memory_text: I gave Gus my copy of 'An Imperial Affliction' and he handed me a novelization of his favorite video game, and when I took it, our hands got tangled for a brief, charged moment—it felt like a real connection.
grounded_facts: Gus gives Hazel a novelization of his favorite video game in exchange for her reading 'An Imperial Affliction', forming a symbolic pact.
Their hands briefly tangle when exchanging books, creating a moment of romantic tension and connection.

cumulative_memories.memory_text: Down in his basement bedroom, I sat on the bed while Gus sat beside me, and we started talking—really talking—about my favorite book and what it means to me, and I remember feeling both exposed and seen.
grounded_facts: Gus and Hazel have an intimate conversation in his basement bedroom after being introduced to his parents.

cumulative_memories.memory_text: I explained why my hands were cold, and Gus flirted with me, saying he loves it when I talk medical—he made me feel seen in a whole new way.
grounded_facts: Gus flirts with Hazel by saying he loves it when she talks medical, responding to her explanation of cold hands.
